data.title: Study Links Shorter Sleep Durations with Greater Risks of Mental Distress in Young Adults - American Academy of Sleep Medicine – Association for Sleep Clinicians and Researchers
data.content:
DARIEN, IL – Young adults who get fewer than eight hours of sleep per night have greater risks of psychological distress, a combination of high levels of depressive and anxious symptoms, according to a study in the Sept. 1 issue of the journal SLEEP. [...] In 2007 the U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration estimated that 17.9 percent of young adults between the ages of 18 and 25 years experienced serious psychological distress in the past year. The Australian Bureau of Statistics reported that 26 percent of all young people between 16 and 24 years of age had a mental disorder in 2007. [...] For a copy of the study, “Short sleep duration in prevalent and persistent psychological distress in young adults: the DRIVE study,” or to arrange an interview with an AASM spokesperson, please contact Public Relations Coordinator Emilee McStay at 630-737-9700, ext. 9345, or emcstay@aasm.org.

data.title: Sleep and Mental Health: How Sleep Deprivation Affects Young Adults | PrairieCare
data.content:
Over time, ongoing sleep issues in college students and other young adults can have a serious impact on mental and physical health. One study of 20,000 young adults found that each hour less sleep increased the risk of psychological distress, while longer sleep duration showed no association with distress. [...] For college students, coursework, socializing, and other on-campus activities can make consistent, quality sleep harder. By some estimates, 70 to 96 percent of college students get less than eight hours of sleep each weeknight, and 50 percent get fewer than seven hours.

Young adults who are working, balancing multiple responsibilities, and navigating other major life transitions can face similar challenges.

## Reasons for Insufficient Sleep in Young Adults [...] Research has found that people with mental health concerns have a much harder time falling asleep. Among those with depression, 60.4 percent reported taking longer than usual to fall asleep, while 53.4 percent of those with anxiety took longer to fall asleep.

Sleep changes don’t necessarily mean that someone has a mental health disorder. But persistent sleep changes can be a red flag to pay attention to.

data.title: The Critical Connection between Teens’ Sleep and Mental Health - National Sleep Foundation
data.content: Getting enough quality sleep also helps teens cope with the stress of their evolving physical, social, and emotional worlds. During deep sleep, the brain regulates stress hormones such as cortisol. Teens who consistently get enough sleep (NSF recommends 8-10 hours each night) can be better equipped to cope with stressors and have less risk of developing chronic stress-related mental health issues. What’s troubling is the vast majority of teens, 80% in a recent NSF poll, are not getting enough [...] Beyond its impact on emotional well-being, healthy sleep is crucial for cognitive functioning and academic performance in teenagers. Teens who consistently get enough sleep are better equipped to concentrate, retain information, and excel in school. However, insufficient sleep may lead to difficulties in problem-solving, decision-making, and overall cognitive abilities, which can negatively impact a teen’s academic success and long-term mental well-being. [...] During adolescence, teens are also navigating new behaviors that require decision-making skills and impulse control. Healthy sleep contributes to improved behavior in teens, leading to fewer accidents, reduced substance use, fewer reckless behaviors, and a lower risk of other health problems.

data.title: Sleep Deprivation and Deficiency - How Sleep Affects Your Health | NHLBI, NIH
data.content:
The symptoms of sleep deficiency may differ between children and adults. Children who are sleep deficient might be overly active and have problems paying attention. They also might misbehave, and their school performance can suffer.

Sleep-deficient children may feel angry and impulsive, have mood swings, feel sad or depressed, or lack motivation.

## Sleep and your health [...] IN THIS ARTICLE

Getting enough quality sleep at the right times can help protect your mental health, physical health, quality of life, and safety.

## How do I know if I’m not getting enough sleep?

Sleep deficiency can cause you to feel very tired during the day. You may not feel refreshed and alert when you wake up. Sleep deficiency also can interfere with work, school, driving, and social functioning. [...] The damage from sleep deficiency can happen in an instant (such as a car crash), or it can harm you over time. For example, ongoing sleep deficiency can raise your risk of some chronic health problems. It also can affect how well you think, react, work, learn, and get along with others.

### Mental health benefits

Sleep helps your brain work properly. While you're sleeping, your brain is getting ready for the next day. It's forming new pathways to help you learn and remember information.
